The Reign of Terror. The climactic and most radical phase of the French Revolution from seventeen ninety-three to seventeen ninety-four, during which the revolutionary government, dominated by Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety, executed tens of thousands of perceived enemies of the revolution through mass trials and guillotining. Justified as a necessary measure to purge counter-revolutionaries and traitors, the Terror instead became a machinery of paranoia, revenge, and ideological conformity that consumed even the Revolution's own leaders. Its sudden collapse with Robespierre's death in July seventeen ninety-four, known as Thermidor, illustrated the unsustainability of terror as a governing principle and demonstrated the Revolution's capacity to devour itself.

The Terror emerged from the conviction that internal enemies—aristocrats, clergy, moderates, and foreign spies—threatened the Revolution from within. As external wars went badly, radical factions demanded ruthless measures. The Committee of Public Safety, ostensibly an emergency executive body, became the Terror's engine under Robespierre's dominance, ordering arrests, trials, and executions with minimal legal process. The Revolutionary Tribunal, established in August seventeen ninety-two, conducted rapid trials with predetermined verdicts. Acquittals were rare, and execution was the default sentence.

Victims ranged from aristocrats and counter-revolutionary clergy to moderate revolutionaries—the Girondins rounded up in June seventeen ninety-three—to Robespierre's rivals Danton and Hébert, to ordinary people denounced by neighbors or suspected of insufficient fervor. The guillotine became the symbol of the Terror, claiming an estimated sixteen thousand to forty thousand lives, concentrated in Paris but extending to provincial cities and the Vendée, where peasant uprising was brutally suppressed.

Robespierre invoked virtue, or vertu, as the Revolution's highest good, insisting that terror was virtue's instrument. Enemies of virtue were enemies of the people and must die. The revolutionary government attempted to de-Christianize France through desecration, the arrest of priests, and secular festivals. Suspects were arrested on vague charges—conspiracy, federalism, moderation—interpreted infinitely broadly, with the burden of proof inverted so that accusation alone could trigger execution.

By early seventeen ninety-four, the Terror was consuming its own architects. The radical Hébertists were purged in March seventeen ninety-four, then the moderate Dantonists in April seventeen ninety-four, leaving only Robespierre and his closest allies. Thermidor, on July twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth, seventeen ninety-four, saw Robespierre and his supporters arrested and guillotined, precipitating the rapid dismantling of the Terror's institutions and ending the Revolution's most violent phase.
